title: Nobody Splits the Last Crate
audienceRationale: A 9-year-old who has proven single-step inversion on unseen families needs the next honest rung: deciding WHICH quantity is unknown, coordinating two constraints, and rejecting impossible splits with justification. Branch evidence factually shows he completed a construction/manipulation experience, rated it 5/5, and chose to replay it — treated as an uncertain signal that hands-on manipulation with visible physical consequence lands well, which this dial-and-cargo design leans into without copying any prior game. The preview-assist that fades across the night respects that he doesn't need scaffolding on computation, only on the new synthesis moves; the REFUSE lever gives the biggest sensory reward precisely because rejecting a forced split is the hardest, least-practiced correct action for a child trained to always produce an answer.
openingPromise: You are the only dockhand on the night shift. Six orders are rolling toward the barge and the dispatcher never tells you what's missing — you decide what goes where, and you decide what CANNOT go at all. The barge leaves at dawn with whatever manifest you built.
firstThreeSeconds: A dark rain-slicked cargo dock lights up bay by bay as a low horn sounds. A conveyor rumbles to life and the first crate stack slides into view under a spotlight. The dispatcher radio crackles one line of text, and a big brass BAY dial and a red REFUSE lever rise from the console — both glowing, both touchable immediately.
firstAction: The child grabs the brass dial and spins it. As it turns, ghost-outline bays appear or vanish on the dock in real time, and the crate stack pre-splits into translucent preview groups that grow or shrink live — so within one spin the child sees that the dial IS the math. Releasing the dial and pulling the green SHIP handle commits the split and crates physically ride the conveyor into the bays.
interactionDemonstration: Order 1 walkthrough: dispatcher says '72 crates arriving. Dock has 9 bays. Fill them even.' The child spins the dial to 6 — nine ghost bays each show 6 translucent crates, but the pile above shows 18 leftover ghosts flickering amber. Dial to 9 — bays bulge past their chalk lines, amber buzz. Dial to 8 — all nine ghost stacks snap flush, gold hum. Pull SHIP: 72 real crates ride the conveyor, load nine bays in eight-beat pulses, doors seal clunk-hiss ×9, barge dips lower, dispatcher: 'Clean. Didn't expect that.' The manifest stamps line one in gold.
coreInteraction: Each of six orders arrives as a one-line dispatcher message that never labels the unknown (e.g., "56 crates. Every bay takes 8." vs "63 crates across 9 bays. Load them."). The child must first decide which quantity is missing, then set it with the brass dial. A live preview shows translucent crates distributing into ghost bays as the dial turns — equal stacks glow steady gold; an uneven preview flickers amber with one bay visibly short or bulging. The child can trust the preview or ignore it. Committing with the SHIP handle sends real crates down the conveyor: correct splits load clean and the bay doors seal with a satisfying clunk-hiss; wrong splits load anyway, one bay ends up short or overflowing, the horn blares, and the order sails with a torn hole stamped in the manifest. For impossible orders (e.g., 58 crates into 8 bays), no dial position ever produces steady gold — the honest move is slamming the REFUSE lever, after which the dock ledger slides up and asks the child to set the two nearby totals that WOULD have worked (56 and 64), proving the refusal with math rather than a guess.
mathAsPower: The dial value is a factor and the dock renders the multiplication live: bays × crates-per-bay materializes as physical geometry the child can read at a glance. Recovering the missing factor is literally steering cargo — dial 7 when the total is 63 across 9 bays and the stacks land flush and seal; dial 8 and a bay overflows onto the dock, crates tumbling into the water. Impossibility is visible power too: on a 58-into-8-bays order, sweeping the full dial shows every configuration flicker uneven — the child watches the number line refuse to cooperate, then wields the REFUSE lever as the mathematically correct action and defends it by dialing the two neighboring multiples that seal clean. Math never decorates a button; math is the loading mechanism, the failure mechanism, and the proof mechanism.
stakes: Every order ships one way or another — there is no retry-until-perfect on a committed order. A wrong split doesn't vanish; the crates load badly, the horn blows, and a torn hole is stamped permanently into the night's manifest. Forcing an impossible split is the worst outcome: crates spill into the harbor and the hole is stamped in red. The manifest is the score, the story, and the receipt, and it is read aloud at dawn.
consequences: Under-split: one bay sits visibly short, its door refuses to seal, and the bay light burns amber all night in the background of subsequent orders — mistakes stay on screen. Over-split: crates overflow, tumble off the dock edge with splashes, and the overflow count is written on the manifest hole ('3 crates lost'). Shipping an impossible order: the barge accepts it but the dispatcher radio goes silent for a beat, then reads back the broken math flatly ('9 bays of 8 is 72. 9 bays of 9 is 81. You sent 80.') — the world itself states the multiplication that proves the error. Refusing a POSSIBLE order costs too: the crates sit stranded on the dock and the ledger shows the split that would have worked, so refusal is never a safe default.
recovery: After any holed order, the next conveyor pause offers a 'PATCH SLIP': the child may dial the correct value once, unpressured, onto the ledger — it doesn't un-tear the hole, but it converts the hole from red to gray ('understood, logged') and restores the dock lights to full. Recovery is thus a second act of the same math, not a freebie. If the child refuses two possible orders in a row (over-refusing), the foreman walks over and demonstrates one full dial sweep on a simple total, re-anchoring what 'seals clean' looks like before the next order arrives.
progression: Order 1 — WARM STEEL: '72 crates arriving. Dock has 9 bays. Fill them even.' Unknown is crates-per-bay. Single inversion on an unseen family (9s). Full preview assistance; teaches the dial-preview-ship loop.

Order 2 — FLIPPED UNKNOWN: '48 crates. Every bay holds 6. How many bays do I open?' Same total-first phrasing but the OTHER quantity is missing; the child must notice the unknown switched. Preview still live.

Order 3 — FIRST IMPOSSIBLE, UNDISGUISED: '58 crates into 8 bays. Dispatcher says make it work.' No dial value seals. The REFUSE lever pulses faintly after a full dial sweep. Ledger asks for the two nearby workable totals (56 and 64) by dialing them onto the ledger scale, which balances visually when correct.

Order 4 — DIM PREVIEW: '63 crates across some bays of 7' — preview ghosts are now faded to near-invisible and the flicker warning is gone; the child must compute before committing rather than dial-hunting. Unknown could be either; wording forces interpretation.

Order 5 — DOUBLE CONSTRAINT: '84 crates. No bay may hold fewer than 9. Choose your bay count.' The child must find a bay count where 84 splits evenly AND each stack meets the minimum — multiple dial values split evenly (e.g., 12 bays of 7 fails the minimum; 7 bays of 12 or fewer bays work). Two constraints, one dial, real reasoning about which factor pair survives both rules.

Order 6 — THE IMPOSSIBLE ONE DRESSED EASY: '80 crates, 9 bays, easy money — 9s are your best table, kid.' Friendly framing, round-looking total, no preview at all. 80 is not a multiple of 9. Shipping it tears the biggest hole yet; refusing it and naming 72 and 81 on the ledger seals the night with a golden stamp.

DAWN MANIFEST: The full ledger unrolls — every clean seal, every justified refusal, every hole — read back line by line as the barge pulls out. Then the foreman asks one question with two real buttons: 'Take tomorrow's shift?'
interactionContinuity: One console, all night: dial + SHIP handle + REFUSE lever never change, so escalation comes from the math (unknown-type switching, fading previews, double constraints, disguised impossibility), never from new controls. Holed and sealed bays from earlier orders remain visible in every subsequent shot, so the night is one continuous place, not six disconnected problems. The ledger accumulates in the corner all shift and becomes the finale.
worldReaction: The dock is a live ledger of the child's math. Sealed bays glow warm gold and their crane arms salute; holed bays stay amber with a slow drip of rain; refused orders stack neatly under a REFUSED tarp with the two proven-workable totals chalked on the side. The barge visibly rides lower in the water as correct cargo loads. The dispatcher's radio tone shifts across the night — clipped and skeptical early, warm and conversational after clean seals, dead silent after a forced impossible split. At dawn, seagulls land only on sealed bays.
payoff: The Dawn Manifest sequence: the barge horn sounds long and low, the ledger unrolls across the whole screen, and each line is stamped in order — clean seals in gold, justified refusals in silver with their two workable neighbors shown, holes in gray or red. A perfect night (all six handled correctly, both impossibles refused and proven) earns the DOCKMASTER'S KEY, a brass key that visibly hangs on the console in any replay. Regardless of outcome, the foreman's final question — 'Take tomorrow's shift?' — hands the child genuine agency over replay, honoring the manifest as earned history rather than a grade.
replayVariation: Tomorrow's shift regenerates all six orders from fresh unseen families (7s, 8s, 9s, totals to 90) with the unknown-type sequence reshuffled and the impossible orders relocated — the child can never memorize 'order 3 is the trap.' Impossible totals are drawn to sit exactly between two multiples of the demanded bay count so the two-neighbor justification always exists. On a replay after earning the Dockmaster's Key, previews are off from order 1 and a rare seventh 'RUSH ORDER' can appear with a double constraint AND a hidden impossibility, keeping veterans honest.
visualDirection: Warm-noir night dock: deep navy sky, rain-streaked reflections on wet planks, sodium-orange work lamps, brass and rivet console in the foreground. Crates are chunky, high-contrast, individually countable at a glance — no stack ever hides its count. Bay outlines are chalk-white ghosts during preview, solid steel when committed. Typography on the dispatcher line is a bold stencil face sized for a 9-year-old reading one line fast. Color is semantic and consistent: gold = sealed/true, amber = uneven/warning, red = forced impossibility, silver = proven refusal. Everything important is readable in silhouette.
motionDirection: The dial has weighted, notched rotation with slight overshoot and settle. Preview crates redistribute with a quick elastic shuffle on every dial notch — the redistribution IS the multiplication animating. Committed crates ride the conveyor with individual bob and clatter, load bays in rhythmic pulses (one pulse per crate-per-bay, so the child can literally count the beat), and bay doors seal with a two-stage clunk-hiss. Overflow crates tumble with real-feeling physics into water splashes. The REFUSE lever throws with a heavy ka-CHUNK and a full-screen stamp slam. The dawn ledger unrolls with paper physics and each stamp lands with screen-shake proportional to its weight.
soundDirection: Bed: low rain, distant harbor bells, conveyor rumble that ducks under the dispatcher radio. The dial clicks in musical notches that rise in pitch with the value — the child can almost hear the factor. Equal-split preview hums a soft consonant chord; uneven preview buzzes a flat dissonant tone with the short bay's position panned to its side. Clean seal: clunk-hiss plus a small brass fanfare note per sealed bay. Horn on a holed shipment is long, low, and mournful — consequence, not punishment. REFUSE lever gets the biggest, most satisfying sound in the game (heavy metal throw + stamp slam) so that correct refusal FEELS powerful, not like giving up. Dawn manifest is read over a slow warm piano figure.
usefulLibraries: GSAP (dial settle, conveyor choreography, ledger unroll, stamp slams)
Howler.js (layered dock ambience, pitch-mapped dial clicks, spatialized bay warnings)
PixiJS (rain, wet-plank reflections, spotlight compositing at 60fps)
engagementPrediction: High initial pull from the tactile dial-preview loop (visible cause-effect within 3 seconds of touching the dial). The pitch-mapped dial clicks and pulse-counted loading give computation a sensory payoff on every order. Predicted friction point: order 6's disguised impossibility after a no-preview order 4 — some frustration is intended and productive; the PATCH SLIP recovery and the non-judgmental dawn read-back keep failure narratively absorbed rather than punitive. The 'take tomorrow's shift?' choice plus regenerated orders is predicted to convert the ending into voluntary replay, consistent with (but not dependent on) the observed replay_same behavior.
falsifyingEvidence: The design fails if logs show: (a) dial-sweep hunting — the child sweeping every dial value watching for gold on orders 1–3 and never pre-committing a value, indicating preview-reading replaced computation (mitigated by order-4 preview fade, but if accuracy collapses exactly when previews fade, the earlier orders taught nothing); (b) REFUSE used as a default on ≥3 possible orders, indicating the lever's big reward taught avoidance rather than justified rejection; (c) neighbor-total justification answered by ±1-dial trial-and-error on the ledger scale rather than stated multiples, indicating the impossibility proof is being brute-forced; (d) order-5 double constraint solved only by exhaustive dialing with no evidence of eliminating factor pairs. Any of these would falsify the claim that this artifact measures synthesis rather than interface exploitation.
